expectedText:
COASTAL DEVELOPMENT PERMIT REQUIREMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Ocean Ave. · San Luis Obispo

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law on the coastal development permit requirement created by the California Coastal Act of 1976, Public Resources Code section 30000 et seq., as it may relate to real property at 123 Ocean Ave., San Luis Obispo County, California (Assessor's Parcel Number 012-345-678), owned by Jane Doe, in connection with the following proposed activity: construction of a new single-family residence. It states what California law provides about which activities count as "development" under the Coastal Act, the geographic "coastal zone" the Act applies within, which agency (the California Coastal Commission or a local government implementing a certified Local Coastal Program) has permitting authority over a given development at a given time, the statute's own listed exemptions from the permit requirement, and the civil penalties the statute states for a violation. It is separate from, and does not substitute for, the California Environmental Quality Act review, any Subdivision Map Act approval (final map, parcel map, or lot line adjustment), any local zoning or building permit, or any other state, regional, or local permit that may separately apply to the same activity. This information sheet is not itself a coastal development permit application, and it does not tell Jane Doe, John Smith, or any other person whether the described activity requires a coastal development permit, which agency currently holds permitting jurisdiction over 123 Ocean Ave., or whether any statutory exemption applies to it.

THE STATUTORY "COASTAL ZONE"
The Coastal Act's permit requirement applies only within a defined geographic area the statute calls the "coastal zone." Public Resources Code section 30103(a) defines that zone as the land and water area of California from the Oregon border to the Mexican border, extending seaward to the state's outer limit of jurisdiction and including all offshore islands, and states a general inland extent of 1,000 yards from the mean high tide line of the sea. The same subdivision states that in significant coastal estuarine, habitat, and recreational areas the zone extends inland further — to the first major ridgeline paralleling the sea or five miles from the mean high tide line, whichever is less — while in developed urban areas the zone generally extends inland less than 1,000 yards. Section 30103(b) separately gives the Coastal Commission authority to prepare a detailed map of the zone and to adjust its inland or seaward boundary within stated limits to avoid bisecting a single lot or parcel.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Coastal zone” means that land and water area of the State of California from the Oregon border to the border of the Republic of Mexico, specified on the maps identified and set forth in Section 17 of Chapter 1330 of the Statutes of 1976, extending seaward to the state’s outer limit of jurisdiction, including all offshore islands, and extending inland generally 1,000 yards from the mean high tide line of the sea."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30103(a), California Public Resources Code, definition of "coastal zone" — general extent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30103.)
  "In significant coastal estuarine, habitat, and recreational areas it extends inland to the first major ridgeline paralleling the sea or five miles from the mean high tide line of the sea, whichever is less, and in developed urban areas the zone generally extends inland less than 1,000 yards."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30103(a), California Public Resources Code, definition of "coastal zone" — extended and urban-area boundaries (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30103.)
  Known gap: Section 30103(a)'s own text states that the coastal zone's precise boundary is fixed by maps — those identified in Section 17 of Chapter 1330 of the Statutes of 1976, and the more detailed map the Commission adopts under subdivision (b) — not solely by the general distance figures quoted above; this clause quotes those general distance rules and does not itself examine any map to determine whether a particular parcel lies within the coastal zone. The statute also excludes the separate area of jurisdiction of the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission from the coastal zone, a carve-out this clause states exists but does not independently evaluate for this property. The two quotations below are both drawn from subdivision (a) of the same section and are not independent of each other. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines its coastal zone — not a claim about which jurisdiction's coastal management law applies to a particular property.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "DEVELOPMENT"
The coastal development permit requirement applies to activity that falls within the Coastal Act's own, broader-than-colloquial definition of "development." Public Resources Code section 30106 defines "development" to include placing or erecting solid material or structures; discharging or disposing of dredged material or waste; grading, removing, dredging, mining, or extracting materials; a change in the density or intensity of use of land — expressly including subdivision under the Subdivision Map Act and any other division of land, including lot splits (subject to a stated exception for a land division brought about by a public agency's purchase for public recreational use); a change in the intensity of use of water or access to it; and construction, reconstruction, demolition, or alteration of the size of any structure, including a utility facility. The statute separately includes the removal or harvesting of major vegetation, subject to stated exceptions for agricultural purposes, kelp harvesting, and timber operations conducted under a Z'berg-Nejedly Forest Practice Act timber harvesting plan. Section 30106 also states that "structure" includes, without limitation, a building, road, pipe, flume, conduit, siphon, aqueduct, telephone line, and electrical power transmission and distribution line.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Development” means, on land, in or under water, the placement or erection of any solid material or structure; discharge or disposal of any dredged material or of any gaseous, liquid, solid, or thermal waste; grading, removing, dredging, mining, or extraction of any materials; change in the density or intensity of use of land, including, but not limited to, subdivision pursuant to the Subdivision Map Act (commencing with Section 66410 of the Government Code), and any other division of land, including lot splits, except where the land division is brought about in connection with the purchase of such land by a public agency for public recreational use; change in the intensity of use of water, or of access thereto; construction, reconstruction, demolition, or alteration of the size of any structure, including any facility of any private, public, or municipal utility"
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30106, California Public Resources Code, definition of "development" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30106.)
  Known gap: The quotation below reproduces section 30106's definition through its structure-alteration clause; it omits the statute's separate vegetation-removal clause and the immediately following sentence defining "structure," both of which this body text paraphrases rather than quotes. This clause does not determine whether any specific described activity falls within this definition, and it does not address the Subdivision Map Act's own separate approval procedure (Government Code section 66410 et seq.) that section 30106 cross-references only to establish that a Map Act subdivision counts as Coastal Act "development." This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines "development" for coastal permitting purposes — not a claim about which jurisdiction's land-use law applies to a particular activity.

GENERAL PERMIT REQUIREMENT
Public Resources Code section 30600(a) states that, except as provided in subdivision (e) and in addition to any other permit required by law from any local government or state, regional, or local agency, any person wishing to perform or undertake development in the coastal zone must obtain a coastal development permit. Section 30600(e) separately states that the section does not apply to certain emergency work and certain emergency highway repairs, subject to a 14-day post-commencement notification requirement to the Commission. Which agency issues the coastal development permit depends on the status of the local government's Local Coastal Program: section 30600(b) and (c) describe a local government's option, before its Local Coastal Program is certified, to establish its own permit procedures for development within its jurisdiction (subject to statutory limits), with the Commission or the local government issuing the permit depending on whether that option is exercised; and section 30600(d) states that, after certification of its Local Coastal Program, a coastal development permit is obtained from the local government as provided in section 30519.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (e), and in addition to obtaining any other permit required by law from any local government or from any state, regional, or local agency, any person, as defined in Section 21066, wishing to perform or undertake any development in the coastal zone, other than a facility subject to Section 25500, shall obtain a coastal development permit."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30600(a), California Public Resources Code, general coastal development permit requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30600.)
  "After certification of its local coastal program or pursuant to the provisions of Section 30600.5, a coastal development permit shall be obtained from the local government as provided for in Section 30519 or Section 30600.5."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30600(d), California Public Resources Code, permit issuance after Local Coastal Program certification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30600.)
  Known gap: This clause states section 30600's own general structure; it does not determine, for any specific parcel, whether the local government in whose jurisdiction that parcel lies has a certified Local Coastal Program, has exercised the pre-certification permitting option under subdivision (b), or otherwise currently holds permitting authority under subdivision (d) — a fact-specific determination this clause does not make. The two quotations below are subsections (a) and (d) of the same statutory section; this clause does not separately quote subsections (b) and (c), which are described only in narrative form above. Section 30600(a)'s reference to "any person, as defined in Section 21066" incorporates a Public Resources Code definition (from a different division, the California Environmental Quality Act) that this clause does not itself reproduce or verify. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions interpreting the scope of this permit requirement returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (daily quota exhausted); no case law was reviewed for this clause, which rests on the statutory text of section 30600 alone. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal permitting framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property or activity.

ADDITIONAL COMMISSION PERMIT REQUIREMENT IN SENSITIVE AREAS
Before a Local Coastal Program is certified, Public Resources Code section 30601 requires a coastal development permit from the Commission itself — in addition to, not instead of, any local government permit under section 30600(b) or (d) — for development in certain geographically sensitive locations. Those locations include development between the sea and the first public road paralleling the sea, or within 300 feet of the inland extent of any beach or of the mean high tide line where there is no beach, whichever distance is greater; development on tidelands, submerged lands, or public trust lands, or within 100 feet of a wetland, estuary, or stream, or within 300 feet of the top of the seaward face of a coastal bluff, if not already covered by the first category; and any development that constitutes a major public works project or a major energy facility.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Prior to certification of the local coastal program and, where applicable, in addition to a permit from local government pursuant to subdivision (b) or (d) of Section 30600, a coastal development permit shall be obtained from the commission for any of the following: (1) Developments between the sea and the first public road paralleling the sea or within 300 feet of the inland extent of any beach or of the mean high tide line of the sea where there is no beach, whichever is the greater distance."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30601(1), California Public Resources Code, Commission permit jurisdiction — shoreline and beach areas (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30601.)
  "(2) Developments not included within paragraph (1) located on tidelands, submerged lands, public trust lands, within 100 feet of any wetland, estuary, stream, or within 300 feet of the top of the seaward face of any coastal bluff."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30601(2), California Public Resources Code, Commission permit jurisdiction — tidelands, wetlands, and bluffs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30601.)
  Known gap: This clause states section 30601 as it stood after its 1981 amendment; it does not verify whether any later amendment has changed this text, and it does not determine, for any specific property, whether that property in fact lies within any of the described distance zones from the sea, a beach, a wetland, an estuary, a stream, or a coastal bluff — a factual, often survey-dependent determination this clause does not make. The two quotations below are paragraphs (1) and (2) of the same statutory sentence, not independent sources. This clause also does not address whether or how this additional Commission jurisdiction changes once a Local Coastal Program is certified for the area, a topic addressed in the following clause. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal permitting framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property.

DELEGATION TO LOCAL GOVERNMENT AFTER CERTIFICATION
Public Resources Code section 30519(a) states that once a Local Coastal Program, or a portion of one, has been certified and all implementing actions in the affected area have become effective, the development review authority described in Chapter 7 of the Coastal Act (the coastal development permit chapter) is no longer exercised by the Commission over new development in that area, and is instead delegated to the local government implementing the program — subject to a stated exception for appeals to the Commission under section 30603. Section 30519(b) states that this delegation does not apply to development on tidelands, submerged lands, or public trust lands, nor to development within ports covered by a separate statutory chapter or within a state university or college in the coastal zone, with a further exception restoring delegation for a port or harbor district's or authority's development on legislatively granted lands where the certified Local Coastal Program includes that district's or authority's specific development plans.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "after a local coastal program, or any portion thereof, has been certified and all implementing actions within the area affected have become effective, the development review authority provided for in Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 30600) shall no longer be exercised by the commission over any new development proposed within the area to which the certified local coastal program, or any portion thereof, applies and shall at that time be delegated to the local government that is implementing the local coastal program or any portion thereof."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30519(a), California Public Resources Code, delegation of coastal permit authority to local government (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30519.)
  Known gap: This clause does not determine, for any specific property, whether the local government with jurisdiction over that property has in fact certified a Local Coastal Program covering it, or whether all implementing actions for that program have become effective — both preconditions to this delegation under the statute's own terms. It also does not evaluate whether a particular property falls within any of section 30519(b)'s stated exceptions (tidelands, submerged or public trust lands, ports, or a state university or college). This clause quotes only subdivision (a); subdivision (b)'s exceptions and subdivision (c)'s separate provision allowing the Commission to recommend program amendments for uses of greater-than-local importance are described above only in narrative form. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California allocates coastal permitting authority between a state commission and local government — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property.

STATUTORY EXEMPTIONS FROM THE PERMIT REQUIREMENT
The Coastal Act lists categories of activity for which no coastal development permit is required. Public Resources Code section 30600(e) exempts specified emergency work — immediate emergency work to protect life or property, and certain emergency highway repairs undertaken within one year of storm, fire, flood, earthquake, or similar damage — subject to a 14-day post-commencement notification to the Commission and excluding highway-widening or -expansion projects. Separately, section 30610 lists further exemptions, including improvements to an existing single-family residence, subject to the Commission's own regulatory authority to require a permit for classes of improvement that involve a risk of adverse environmental effect; repair or maintenance activity that does not add to, enlarge, or expand the object being repaired or maintained, subject to a similar Commission regulatory carve-out for extraordinary repair methods that risk substantial adverse environmental impact; certain improvements to non-single-family structures; maintenance dredging of existing navigation channels under an Army Corps of Engineers permit; installation of certain utility connections to already-approved development; replacement, within stated size and siting limits, of a structure destroyed by disaster; and other categories the statute itself lists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Improvements to existing single-family residences; provided, however, that the commission shall specify, by regulation, those classes of development which involve a risk of adverse environmental effect and shall require that a coastal development permit be obtained pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30610(a), California Public Resources Code, exemption for improvements to an existing single-family residence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30610.)
  "Repair or maintenance activities that do not result in an addition to, or enlargement or expansion of, the object of those repair or maintenance activities; provided, however, that if the commission determines that certain extraordinary methods of repair and maintenance involve a risk of substantial adverse environmental impact, it shall, by regulation, require that a permit be obtained pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30610(d), California Public Resources Code, exemption for repair or maintenance activity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30610.)
  Known gap: Section 30610 lists more exemption categories than this clause's two quoted subsections; subdivisions (b), (c), (e), (f), (g), (h), and (i) are described only in narrative summary above and are not independently quoted. Both quoted exemptions — subdivisions (a) and (d) — are themselves qualified by the Commission's own regulatory authority to pull a class of development back into the permit requirement; this clause does not check whether the Commission has adopted such a regulation for any specific class of improvement or repair, and it does not determine whether any particular described activity in fact falls within any exemption listed here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal-permit exemption structure — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular activity.

CIVIL PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
Public Resources Code section 30820 states civil liability for a Coastal Act violation. Under subdivision (a)(1), a superior court may impose civil liability, in an amount not less than $500 and not more than $30,000, on a person who performs or undertakes development that violates the Coastal Act or is inconsistent with a previously issued coastal development permit. Under subdivision (a)(2), civil liability up to $30,000 may be imposed for any other Coastal Act violation. Subdivision (b) states a separate, higher-exposure liability for a person who intentionally and knowingly performs or undertakes development in violation of the Act or inconsistent with a previously issued permit: liability of not less than $1,000 nor more than $15,000 per day for each day the violation persists. Subdivision (c) lists factors a court considers in setting the amount of civil liability, including the nature and gravity of the violation, whether it can be remedied, the sensitivity of the affected resource, the state's cost of bringing the action, and, as to the violator, any voluntary remedial measures, prior violation history, culpability, and any resulting economic profit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Civil liability may be imposed by the superior court in accordance with this article on any person who performs or undertakes development that is in violation of this division or that is inconsistent with any coastal development permit previously issued by the commission, a local government that is implementing a certified local coastal program, or a port governing body that is implementing a certified port master plan, in an amount that shall not exceed thirty thousand dollars ($30,000) and shall not be less than five hundred dollars ($500)."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30820(a)(1), California Public Resources Code, civil liability for a Coastal Act violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30820.)
  "when the person intentionally and knowingly performs or undertakes the development in violation of this division or inconsistent with any previously issued coastal development permit, may, in addition to any other penalties, be civilly liable in accordance with this subdivision. Civil liability may be imposed by the superior court in accordance with this article for a violation as specified in this subdivision in an amount which shall not be less than one thousand dollars ($1,000), nor more than fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000), per day for each day in which the violation persists."
  — Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30820(b), California Public Resources Code, enhanced civil liability for an intentional and knowing violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=30820.)
  Known gap: This clause states the civil-liability structure of section 30820 alone; the Coastal Act contains separate provisions elsewhere in the same chapter for injunctive relief, cease-and-desist orders, restoration orders, and criminal penalties, none of which this clause quotes or describes. The dollar figures quoted are those stated in the current text of section 30820 as fetched; this clause does not track any subsequent legislative amendment to those figures. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific activity in fact violates the Coastal Act or is inconsistent with any permit. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions applying this penalty provision returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (daily quota exhausted) before any search could be completed; no case law was reviewed for this clause. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own Coastal Act enforcement framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs particular conduct.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Jane Doe and John Smith acknowledge that they have reviewed this information sheet describing California's coastal development permit requirement under the Coastal Act, and understand that it states general California statutory law rather than a determination about 123 Ocean Ave. or about construction of a new single-family residence.

Signature of John Smith: _________________________ Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: Public Resources Code section 30519(a) states that once a Local Coastal Program, or a portion of one, has been certified and all implementing actions in the affected area have become effective, the development review authority described in Chapter 7 of the Coastal Act (the coastal development permit chapter) is no longer exercised by the Commission over new development in that area, and is instead delegated to the local government implementing the program — subject to a stated exception for appeals to the Commission under section 30603. Section 30519(b) states that this delegation does not apply to development on tidelands, submerged lands, or public trust lands, nor to development within ports covered by a separate statutory chapter or within a state university or college in the coastal zone, with a further exception restoring delegation for a port or harbor district's or authority's development on legislatively granted lands where the certified Local Coastal Program includes that district's or authority's specific development plans.

citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, delegation of coastal permit authority to local government
citations.quote: after a local coastal program, or any portion thereof, has been certified and all implementing actions within the area affected have become effective, the development review authority provided for in Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 30600) shall no longer be exercised by the commission over any new development proposed within the area to which the certified local coastal program, or any portion thereof, applies and shall at that time be delegated to the local government that is implementing the local coastal program or any portion thereof.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not determine, for any specific property, whether the local government with jurisdiction over that property has in fact certified a Local Coastal Program covering it, or whether all implementing actions for that program have become effective — both preconditions to this delegation under the statute's own terms. It also does not evaluate whether a particular property falls within any of section 30519(b)'s stated exceptions (tidelands, submerged or public trust lands, ports, or a state university or college). This clause quotes only subdivision (a); subdivision (b)'s exceptions and subdivision (c)'s separate provision allowing the Commission to recommend program amendments for uses of greater-than-local importance are described above only in narrative form. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California allocates coastal permitting authority between a state commission and local government — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property.

expectedJSON.body: The Coastal Act lists categories of activity for which no coastal development permit is required. Public Resources Code section 30600(e) exempts specified emergency work — immediate emergency work to protect life or property, and certain emergency highway repairs undertaken within one year of storm, fire, flood, earthquake, or similar damage — subject to a 14-day post-commencement notification to the Commission and excluding highway-widening or -expansion projects. Separately, section 30610 lists further exemptions, including improvements to an existing single-family residence, subject to the Commission's own regulatory authority to require a permit for classes of improvement that involve a risk of adverse environmental effect; repair or maintenance activity that does not add to, enlarge, or expand the object being repaired or maintained, subject to a similar Commission regulatory carve-out for extraordinary repair methods that risk substantial adverse environmental impact; certain improvements to non-single-family structures; maintenance dredging of existing navigation channels under an Army Corps of Engineers permit; installation of certain utility connections to already-approved development; replacement, within stated size and siting limits, of a structure destroyed by disaster; and other categories the statute itself lists.

citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, exemption for improvements to an existing single-family residence
citations.quote: Improvements to existing single-family residences; provided, however, that the commission shall specify, by regulation, those classes of development which involve a risk of adverse environmental effect and shall require that a coastal development permit be obtained pursuant to this chapter.

citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, exemption for repair or maintenance activity
citations.quote: Repair or maintenance activities that do not result in an addition to, or enlargement or expansion of, the object of those repair or maintenance activities; provided, however, that if the commission determines that certain extraordinary methods of repair and maintenance involve a risk of substantial adverse environmental impact, it shall, by regulation, require that a permit be obtained pursuant to this chapter.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 30610 lists more exemption categories than this clause's two quoted subsections; subdivisions (b), (c), (e), (f), (g), (h), and (i) are described only in narrative summary above and are not independently quoted. Both quoted exemptions — subdivisions (a) and (d) — are themselves qualified by the Commission's own regulatory authority to pull a class of development back into the permit requirement; this clause does not check whether the Commission has adopted such a regulation for any specific class of improvement or repair, and it does not determine whether any particular described activity in fact falls within any exemption listed here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal-permit exemption structure — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular activity.

expectedJSON.body: Public Resources Code section 30820 states civil liability for a Coastal Act violation. Under subdivision (a)(1), a superior court may impose civil liability, in an amount not less than $500 and not more than $30,000, on a person who performs or undertakes development that violates the Coastal Act or is inconsistent with a previously issued coastal development permit. Under subdivision (a)(2), civil liability up to $30,000 may be imposed for any other Coastal Act violation. Subdivision (b) states a separate, higher-exposure liability for a person who intentionally and knowingly performs or undertakes development in violation of the Act or inconsistent with a previously issued permit: liability of not less than $1,000 nor more than $15,000 per day for each day the violation persists. Subdivision (c) lists factors a court considers in setting the amount of civil liability, including the nature and gravity of the violation, whether it can be remedied, the sensitivity of the affected resource, the state's cost of bringing the action, and, as to the violator, any voluntary remedial measures, prior violation history, culpability, and any resulting economic profit.

citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, civil liability for a Coastal Act violation
citations.quote: Civil liability may be imposed by the superior court in accordance with this article on any person who performs or undertakes development that is in violation of this division or that is inconsistent with any coastal development permit previously issued by the commission, a local government that is implementing a certified local coastal program, or a port governing body that is implementing a certified port master plan, in an amount that shall not exceed thirty thousand dollars ($30,000) and shall not be less than five hundred dollars ($500).

citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, enhanced civil liability for an intentional and knowing violation
citations.quote: when the person intentionally and knowingly performs or undertakes the development in violation of this division or inconsistent with any previously issued coastal development permit, may, in addition to any other penalties, be civilly liable in accordance with this subdivision. Civil liability may be imposed by the superior court in accordance with this article for a violation as specified in this subdivision in an amount which shall not be less than one thousand dollars ($1,000), nor more than fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000), per day for each day in which the violation persists.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the civil-liability structure of section 30820 alone; the Coastal Act contains separate provisions elsewhere in the same chapter for injunctive relief, cease-and-desist orders, restoration orders, and criminal penalties, none of which this clause quotes or describes. The dollar figures quoted are those stated in the current text of section 30820 as fetched; this clause does not track any subsequent legislative amendment to those figures. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific activity in fact violates the Coastal Act or is inconsistent with any permit. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own Coastal Act enforcement framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs particular conduct.
